AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) is automatically initiating the five-year reviews (Sunset Reviews) of the antidumping duty (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) orders and suspended investigations listed below. The U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) is publishing concurrently with this notice its notice of
Institution of Five-Year Reviews
which covers the same orders and suspended investigations.
DATES:
Applicable November 2, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Commerce official identified in the
Initiation of Review
section below at
( printed page 68946)
AD/CVD Operations, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230. For information from the ITC, contact Mary Messer, Office of Investigations, U.S. International Trade Commission at (202) 205-3193.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Commerce's procedures for the conduct of Sunset Reviews are set forth in its
Procedures for Conducting Five-Year (Sunset) Reviews of Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Orders, 63 FR 13516 (March 20, 1998) and 70 FR 62061 (October 28, 2005). Guidance on methodological or analytical issues relevant to Commerce's conduct of Sunset Reviews is set forth in
Antidumping Proceedings: Calculation of the Weighted-Average Dumping Margin and Assessment Rate in Certain Antidumping Duty Proceedings; Final Modification, 77 FR 8101 (February 14, 2012).
Initiation of Review

Suspended Investigations

Filing Information
All submissions in these Sunset Reviews must be filed in accordance with Commerce's regulations regarding format, translation, and service of documents. These rules, including electronic filing requirements via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS), can be found at 19 CFR 351.303.
In accordance with section 782(b) of the Act, any party submitting factual information in an AD/CVD proceeding must certify to the accuracy and completeness of that information. Parties must use the certification formats provided in 19 CFR 351.303(g). Commerce intends to reject factual submissions if the submitting party does not comply with applicable revised certification requirements.
Letters of Appearance and Administrative Protective Orders
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.103(d), Commerce will maintain and make available a public service list for these proceedings. Parties wishing to participate in any of these five-year reviews must file letters of appearance as discussed at 19 CFR 351.103(d). To facilitate the timely preparation of the public service list, it is requested that those seeking recognition as interested parties to a proceeding submit an entry of appearance within 10 days of the publication of the Notice of Initiation. Because deadlines in Sunset Reviews can be very short, we urge interested parties who want access to proprietary information under administrative protective order (APO) to file an APO application immediately following publication in the
Federal Register
of this notice of initiation. Commerce's regulations on submission of proprietary information and eligibility to receive access to business proprietary information under APO can be found at 19 CFR 351.304-306. Note that Commerce has temporarily modified certain of its requirements for serving documents containing business proprietary information, until further notice.[1]
Information Required From Interested Parties
Domestic interested parties, as defined in sections 771(9)(C), (D), (E), (F), and (G) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.102(b), wishing to participate in a Sunset Review must respond not later than 15 days after the date of publication in the
Federal Register
of this notice of initiation by filing a notice of intent to participate. The required contents of the notice of intent to participate are set forth at 19 CFR 351.218(d)(1)(ii). In accordance with Commerce's regulations, if we do not receive a notice of intent to participate from at least one domestic interested party by the 15-day deadline, Commerce will automatically revoke the order without further review.[2]
If we receive an order-specific notice of intent to participate from a domestic interested party, Commerce's regulations provide that
all parties
wishing to participate in a Sunset Review must file complete substantive responses not later than 30 days after the date of publication in the
Federal Register
of this notice of initiation. The required contents of a substantive response, on an order-specific basis, are set forth at 19 CFR 351.218(d)(3). Note that certain information requirements differ for respondent and domestic parties. Also, note that Commerce's information requirements are distinct from the ITC 's information requirements. Consult Commerce's regulations for information regarding Commerce's conduct of Sunset Reviews. Consult Commerce's regulations at 19 CFR part 351 for definitions of terms and for other general information concerning antidumping and countervailing duty proceedings at

An electronically filed document must be received successfully in its entirety by ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the day on which it is due.

articles.full_text:
A suburban Chicago man has been sentenced to two years in federal prison for conspiring to stage armed robberies so that the purported victims could apply for U.S. immigration visas reserved for crime victims.
From 2022 to 2024, PARTH NAYI organized and participated in hundreds of staged armed robberies at coffee shops, restaurants, liquor stores, and gas stations throughout the country, including in Chicago and the suburbs of Lombard, Elmwood Park, St. Charles, Hickory Hills, River Grove, Lake Villa, and South Holland.  Nayi worked with others to recruit fake victims, pay off store owners to use their locations, coordinate and pay fake robbers, and coach the bogus victims through the plan.  Thousands of individuals who posed as victims each paid Nayi $5,000 to $30,000 to participate in the scam so that they could later apply for Nonimmigrant U-Visas, which are set aside for foreign nationals who are victims of certain crimes and are helpful to law enforcement in the investigation.
During the staged robberies, individuals acting as robbers brandished what appeared to be firearms, approached the purported victims, and demanded money.  Afterwards, the purported victims submitted forms to local law enforcement to obtain certification that they were victims of a qualifying crime and were helpful in the investigation. Upon receiving the certification, the purported victims then submitted fraudulent U-Visa applications to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services predicated upon their alleged status as robbery victims.

Here is the full story, via Ryan.

articles.title: The Trump administration wants to give married parents money to stay at home. Will it be enough?

articles.full_text:
Erica Hall and her husband knew that raising kids wouldn’t be cheap.
They intentionally had their children five years apart because paying for two in daycare would have been too expensive. When her first child was born, Hall had to self-fund her maternity leave by drawing on savings. And recently, Hall was laid off from her tech job, leaving her at a crossroads.
“Do we move to a lower-cost daycare? What kind of job should I look for? Can I dial back now?” said Hall, who lives in Seattle. And perhaps the most essential of all questions: “Do we need to completely 100% replace my income?”
More American families than ever consist of two working parents: 52% are dual-income households, compared to 31% in 1975, according to the Pew Research Center. Eight out of 10 of these families say the arrangement has been beneficial to their finances.
Despite this shift in family dynamics, the Trump administration has remained focused on an agenda that emphasizes a “traditional” family structure, where one parent stays home to take care of children.
As part of this agenda, the White House is considering a program that would pay parents $9,000 annually to stay at home, using reallocated funds that are now used for federal programs that typically support single mothers and low-income families, according to the New York Times.
The plan was reportedly proffered by JD Vance, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, who has proclaimed himself a defender of “pro-family” policies. The vice-president penned a Wall Street Journal op-ed in 2021 criticizing federal spending on daycare, claiming that “young children from average, healthy homes can be harmed by spending long hours in childcare.”
“It turns out that normal Americans care more about their families than their jobs, and want a family policy that doesn’t shunt their kids into crap daycare so they can enjoy more ‘freedom’ in the paid labor force,” he wrote on social media at the time.
As vice-president, Vance has continued to angle himself as a defender of families. “To the radicals who wish to abolish my family and the thousands and millions of other families across our country, we have a simple message for them: stay the hell away from our kids!” Vance said at the Republican’s midterm convention in September.
But experts and parents who spoke to the Guardian said the proposed program for stay-at-home parents prioritizes a single type of family structure and ignores the flexibility that families need to support themselves and their children.
“Families of all compositions need help right now. All families do. We should not pit families against each other,” said Chandra Childers, a senior policy and economic analyst at the Economic Policy Institute.
For Natalia Goodnow of Pittsburgh, being a stay-at-home mother of two was a temporary choice that allowed her family to save on the cost of childcare while she went back to school and pursued a second master’s degree. After she graduated, she was forced to delay her next job search after graduating because the waitlist for her child’s daycare, like many in the country, had grew significantly after the pandemic.
Now, Goodnow is balancing taking care of her children while also building up her own consulting business, which she believes will afford her flexibility to work around her daughter’s schedule. She doesn’t expect she’ll ever stop working in some capacity.
“I’m not built to be just a stay-at-home parent,” she said,
There’s also a risk to relying on one parent’s income. Even though her family is able to live “somewhat stable” on just her husband’s income, Goodnow said she’s worried that his career as a physician, combined with the responsibility to support the whole family himself, will lead to burnout.
“I have to have a second income stream created to give him flexibility to scale down, because it’s just not sustainable,” she said, pointing out that the proposed $9,000 wouldn’t be enough to match what she would make if she worked.
Jillian Whitlow, a mom of three who is pregnant with her fourth child, wishes at times that she could stay at home to take care of her children, but after launching a successful marketing business, her husband left his job as a mechanic to take care of their kids.
The choice stemmed from practicality. The cost of daycare for her children was greater than their monthly mortgage payment.
Though Whitlow’s family, who live in Texas, is in a better financial place than they’ve ever been, they still feel the pain of rising costs and are still paying off student debt and loans on their mobile home. Still, Whitlow sees the White House’s proposal as an unnecessary interference in personal family decisions.
“I would love it if there was a lot less government in all of our lives,” she said, “I would love it if each individual family had more freedom to make the decisions that they want to make about the best way to raise their families.”
“It should be up to me and my family to make that decision, and not the government pushing me to stay at home,” Goodnow said.
Childcare costs can pose a major financial burden on families. Forty per cent of households, including those that have one parent who works less than full-time, spend an outsized percentage of their income on childcare, according to a recent report from the Georgetown Law Center on Poverty and Inequality.
The White House’s plan, by reallocating federal funds from the Department of Health and Human Services that have typically gone to low-income, single-parent families, could actually making childcare even more expensive or less available, Childers said.
“The minute you start draining resources that go into funding this childcare pool, then rates have to rise on other families, some of whom may already be stretching to make it as it is,” she said.
Recent policy changes by the Trump administration may also indirectly make it harder on American families, said Liz Hipple, a policy expert at the Georgetown Law Center on Poverty and Inequality. Recent pushes to increase the work requirements for Medicaid and Snap benefits, for example, will probably make it harder for some families to support themselves.
Policies that support higher wages or paid parental leave would go much further to support families, she added.
“If the Trump administration was serious about supporting traditional families with one breadwinner, there are plenty of labor policies that they could support,” Hipple said. “Those aren’t the policies that they’re pursuing.”

The average price of health insurance in the Obamacare marketplaces will rise by 13 percent next year, according to an analysis on Friday by KFF, the health research group.
The Trump administration on Friday published new prices for 2027 in 30 states with markets managed by the federal government. Using that data and state figures, KFF calculated the increase nationwide.
…The average cost for the cheapest bronze plan with a high deductible will be about $700 a month for a 50-year-old single person, according to Ms. Cox.
Here is more from the NYT.  Of course that makes the people who can expect to be healthy all the less likely to sign up, given that the enforcement of the mandate, for political reasons, was forced to evolve into something quite weak.  For purposes of context, when the original mandate was more tightly enforced, with actual penalties, the ACA was very unpopular and led to significant political protests.  In essence the benefits to a broad, scattered majority were imposed on a well-identified minority, namely those who signed up because of the mandate.  Trump in his first term relaxed mandate enforcement, thereby politically saving Obamacare at least for a while, but also creating this longer-term problem.
It is striking to me how infrequently I hear Democrats boasting about Obamacare.  They instead prefer to talk as if little or nothing has been done for America’s uninsured.

articles.full_text:
What are the worst MR posts, most illogical, poorly reasoned, low value, inconsistent?
From the Archives, written by ChatGPT:
These are provisional candidates for weak reasoning, selected because there is a specific gap between the evidence and the conclusion. This is not an objective ranking of all 40,326 posts in the downloaded archive. Poor reasoning should also be distinguished from low value: an overstated argument can still be unusually useful to think against.
1. Tyler Cowen — Democracy and the Democrats
October 22, 2022 · Main defect: conflating concern about democratic breakdown with unwillingness to accept electoral defeat. Cowen writes that many Democrats believe:
“democracy works satisfactorily only when it delivers sufficiently low gas prices!”
But two positions are logically distinct:

“Democracy is illegitimate when voters choose policies I dislike.”
“Voters might elect politicians who subsequently weaken democratic institutions.”

These are illustrative formulations, not quotations from the post. The second does not imply the first. Someone can accept an election’s legitimacy while worrying about what its winner will do. The post does not adequately establish which position its targets hold. It then compares a sympathetic account of classical liberalism with an unsympathetic account of Democrats, without applying an equivalent evidentiary test to both. The opening also dismisses certain anticipated objections through an insult. That discourages scrutiny precisely where the argument needs distinctions. Verdict: One of the clearest candidates for an unfairly framed argument. The useful underlying point—that democracy can produce bad outcomes—does not establish the accusation being made. Read the original post
2. Tyler Cowen — What the hell is going on?
May 25, 2016 · Main defect: an elastic psychological explanation supported by loosely connected observations. The central hypothesis is:
“The contemporary world is not very well built for a large chunk of males.”
That is worth investigating. The trouble comes when male economic difficulties, changing gender relations, political anger, violence, and support for quite different political movements are bundled together under “brutes.” Several things remain unestablished:

Are the men experiencing the cited disadvantages the same men driving the political developments?
Does the mechanism explain support for Sanders and Trump in the same way?
What observation would distinguish resistance to a “nicer” world from resentment of economic insecurity or perceived contempt?
What does “nice” mean independently of the author’s preferences?

The label risks doing the explanatory work: people support objectionable politics because they are brutish; their politics then becomes evidence of their brutishness. Credit where due: Cowen explicitly calls the hypothesis uncertain and acknowledges weak evidence. That makes it an honest speculative post, rather than a falsely presented research finding. Verdict: A provocative conjecture that outruns its supporting evidence. The caveats are better than the causal argument. Read the original post
3. Alex Tabarrok — The Gaslighting of Parasite
June 25, 2020 · Main defect: treating a contestable interpretation as an unambiguous demonstration. Film spoilers follow. The pivotal sentence is:
“This is not my judgement it is what the film tells us.”
That is exactly what the review needs to establish. Several inferences are too strong:

A child noticing a smell does not establish that the smell lacks class significance. Material conditions can produce differences that children notice.
The poor family’s dishonesty does not rule out a critique of inequality. A film can depict morally compromised people within an unjust or damaging social structure.
Images of sewage and infestation do not uniquely imply that the filmmaker regards the family as morally filthy.
Other critics reaching a different interpretation does not establish deliberate deception or “gaslighting.”

The strongest version of the review would argue that conventional readings underweight the family’s agency and wrongdoing. Instead, it often claims those observations exclude alternative readings. Verdict: Among the most intellectually stimulating but least securely demonstrated of the reviews considered in this archive analysis. This qualifies the earlier recommendation of the review: it deserved inclusion as provocative criticism. That does not make its claims of interpretive certainty persuasive. Read the original post
4. Tyler Cowen — No, American fascism can’t happen here
March 1, 2018 · Main defect: turning a plausible obstacle into an impossibility claim. The MR excerpt argues:
“American fascism cannot happen anymore because the American government is so large and unwieldy.”
Institutional complexity plausibly makes comprehensive control harder. But the conclusion requires additional premises:

Why must an authoritarian movement control the entire bureaucracy rather than strategically important parts?
Why does administrative fragmentation necessarily constrain coercion rather than sometimes obscure responsibility?
How much control would be sufficient, and what evidence establishes that this threshold cannot be reached?

These are questions about the argument’s structure, independent of whether one thinks a particular American administration qualifies as fascist. The June 16, 2025 retrospective points to institutional resistance and executive setbacks. Those are relevant evidence for constraints. They cannot, by themselves, validate the original categorical impossibility claim. Verdict: A potentially valuable institutional argument weakened by excessive certainty. “Important barriers exist” is much better supported than “cannot happen.” This assessment concerns the argument reproduced on MR; the complete linked Politico essay could not be retrieved for this review. Read the original MR post
5. Alex Tabarrok — The Case for Getting Rid of Borders—Completely
October 13, 2015 · Main defect: moving too quickly from equal moral worth to a particular institutional conclusion. The excerpt argues that foreigners do not possess less inherent moral worth. But that premise alone does not settle whether governments may impose any entry restrictions. Equal moral worth can coexist with arguments about special obligations, institutional responsibilities, competing rights, or consequences. Those arguments might ultimately fail—but they require engagement. Likewise, comparing restrictions on exit with restrictions on entry does not establish their moral equivalence. It poses a question rather than answering it. The longer Atlantic essay, published October 10, 2015, adds economic arguments, so it would be unfair to characterize the case as exclusively moral. Nevertheless, the sweeping dismissal of competing moral frameworks is insufficiently defended. Verdict: Forceful advocacy with a missing argumentative bridge. This is a criticism of the claimed deduction, not a demonstration that open borders is wrong. Read the original MR post
Recurring weaknesses
Across these examples, three weaknesses recur:

Certainty exceeds the argument: “cannot,” “obviously,” and “the film tells us” substitute for establishing the relevant threshold.
Opposing positions receive less charitable treatment: disagreement becomes evidence of bad motives, confused psychology, or inability to face reality.
An interesting mechanism becomes a complete explanation: institutional complexity, male displacement, or equal moral standing is asked to resolve more than it actually establishes.

Allegations of inconsistency across posts require more caution. A changed view, a different context, or a different definition is not necessarily a contradiction. The stronger criticism here is uneven standards of proof within individual arguments. For a rigorous critical essay, the strongest starting points are Democracy and the Democrats and The Gaslighting of Parasite. Both have identifiable logical problems that can be examined without relying on hindsight or agreement with the critic’s politics.

articles.title: Affordability top of mind for voters in final sprint to midterms: ‘I have to pick between medicine or groceries’
articles.summary: Cost of living has loomed over this election cycle as workers and unions champion candidates fighting for higher wages and tackling rising pricesFor millions of Americans heading to the polls on Tuesday, affordability is a constant and worsening issue, and it’s been a prevailing concern this election cycle.In Lorain county, Ohio, Gina Jones and her co-workers at the Lorain county job and family services have been on strike since February 2026, the longest public sector strike in Ohio history and...
articles.full_text:
For millions of Americans heading to the polls on Tuesday, affordability is a constant and worsening issue, and it’s been a prevailing concern this election cycle.
In Lorain county, Ohio, Gina Jones and her co-workers at the Lorain county job and family services have been on strike since February 2026, the longest public sector strike in Ohio history and on pace to break the US record for longest public sector strike.
Ohio voted for Donald Trump in 2024 by more than 5%. As the final day of voting nears, Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown has a slight lead on Republican Senate incumbent Jon Husted in polling, and the economy has been a key factor in the fight.
“They don’t pay a living wage any more. They used to,” Jones said. “Our healthcare coverage has stayed the same, but the cost of it has changed significantly. It used to be $35 a month for a family. In January it’s going to be $600 a month for a family for the same coverage.”
She said as wages have lagged, with starting pay at about $15 an hour, health insurance costs have eaten up any wage gains to the extent that some employees are making less than when they started.
Negotiations for a new union contract broke down with the county, now led by three Republican commissioners, as workers are pushing for a $1 an hour increase to their base pay.
Daniel Petticord, the deputy director of the Lorain county jobs and family services, said in an email “management believes it recognizes the important efforts of our bargaining unit employees while maintaining fiscal responsibility,” and blamed the union for walking away from negotiations.
“We service the clients of Lorain county that are the poorest of the community, and some of the people that work at jobs and family services qualify for those same services,” Jones said. “We’re hoping that with the Ohio governor election, that we get somebody in there who will be in favor of labor and see the fact that people don’t make a living wage in Lorain county any more.”
In Minnesota, Bob Mattila, a special education paraprofessional in Minneapolis and SEIU Local 284 member, is looking for elected officials who will back state legislation that would increase pay for himself and his co-workers to $25 an hour and to lower their costs for health insurance.
“We simply aren’t paid enough to do the vitally important work that we do,” Mattila said. “I even take state health insurance because they decided I don’t make enough money.
“Money, power and respect. Those three things are critical to what we need out of our work and what we deserve from our elected officials,” he added. “Having very labor-friendly people in places of power is going to give workers like me things that we need to live, because we’re at a point where I can’t afford to put $50 of gas every time when I fill up my car when I’m not even making $25 an hour.”
Labor leaders see a real advantage for Democrats now that so much focus is on the economy.
“The labor movement’s been talking about the issues that affect workers and the kitchen table for decades, and we’re now seeing that everybody else got the memo,” said Liz Shuler, president of the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US, which has been pushing to turn out 16 million union family voters this election.
“It’s pervasive. Everywhere I travel, every campaign that you see is talking about what working people are struggling through, and it’s the cost of gas, groceries, rent and healthcare, but it’s also the fact that our pay just can’t keep up with the rising prices.”
In Detroit, Michigan, another key battleground state, 27-year-old Bailee Porter, who has worked at Detroit Diesel and is a member of the United Auto Workers, has been canvassing for candidates such as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for the US Senate, citing his support for Medicare for All, which the UAW has also backed.
She said rising prices of basic necessities have made budgeting and cutting back on essentials like groceries a common worry.
“It’s just costly on every aspect. It’s disrupting people’s routines, so it’s ridiculous. Food, gas. I don’t even want to talk about utility bills. It’s just insane,” said Porter. “Things should be affordable. Your basic necessities have to be affordable. There’s just no other way around it. They have to be. Legislation needs to be changed or enforced or written to where it can help the middle class and labor.”
But the financial struggles experienced by many Americans are unlikely to be easily alleviated no matter who wins the midterms. Joe Biden, the US’s most pro-labor president in recent history, also failed to appease voters who were feeling left behind.
Researchers have noted the federal government’s definition of and tracking of poverty doesn’t account for the struggles Americans are facing, as the federal poverty line is outdated from the 1960s and doesn’t account for geographic discrepancies in costs of living.
“The percent of people that are struggling is so much higher than our official statistics are revealing,” said Dr Stephanie Hoopes, an economist and director of United for Alice. “These are often people who are keeping our economy running smoothly and fueling our economic growth, and yet they’re struggling to support their own families.”
- 41.3% of US households, more than 54.5m households, faced financial hardship in 2024, according to a 2026 report by United for Alice.
- 12.5% of US households made under the federal poverty level threshold, an income of $15,060 annually for a single individual and $31,200 for a family of four.
- 28.8% of US households were Alice: asset limited, income constrained and employed. These households earn above the federal poverty level but did not make enough money to afford basic expenses in the county where they live.
- 2025 and 2026 projected data shows the costs of basic necessities continuing to outpace overall inflation.
“By some measures, our economy is doing great, unemployment rate is low, stock markets booming, productivity and GDP are growing,” Hoopes added. “But when you look at things like how many households are Alice [asset limited, income constrained and employed], and that number continuing to increase, and wages lagging behind the cost of living, there’s some real concerns in the economy.”
For Shunda Whitfield, a certified nursing assistant in St Louis, Missouri, those economic concerns can be life-threatening.
She has been struggling with a recent spike in costs for her medication for lupus, an autoimmune disease.
“I sometimes have to choose between if I’m going to get my medication or if I’m going to get groceries in house due to the fact that my medicine is going up,” said Whitfield, who has been struggling to afford a recent spike in costs for her lupus medication.
“You have to juggle things around to make sure you have cash to get to work to make the money to afford groceries or your medication,” she added. “I would like to see people get out here and vote to put people in place that are for the working people and not just for the billionaires.”
